deal_breakers.title: Asymmetric Termination Rights
deal_breakers.claim: The Provider has the right to terminate for convenience with a 15-day notice, while the Customer can only terminate for convenience after 12 months with a 60-day notice.
deal_breakers.plain_english: The Provider has the right to terminate for convenience with a 15-day notice, while the Customer can only terminate for convenience after 12 months with a 60-day notice.
deal_breakers.why_flagged: The differing notice periods and conditions for termination for convenience create an imbalance in the rights of the parties, potentially disadvantaging the Customer.
deal_breakers.suggested_negotiation: Consider aligning the termination rights and notice periods for both parties to ensure fairness and balance in the agreement.

clause_balance.provider_terms: Can terminate for convenience at any time upon 15 days' notice.
clause_balance.customer_terms: Can terminate for convenience only after 12 months and upon 60 days' notice.
clause_balance.asymmetry_summary: Severe asymmetry: Provider can exit after 15 days; Customer is locked in for 12 months with 60-day notice.

evidence.quote: Provider may terminate this Agreement for convenience at any time upon 15 days’ written notice to Customer.
Customer may terminate for convenience only after the first 12 months of the Term and upon 60 days’ written notice.

deal_breakers.title: Aggregate Liability Cap and Coverage Duration
deal_breakers.claim: The aggregate liability cap is limited to the fees paid or payable by Customer to Provider during the three months preceding the event giving rise to the claim.
deal_breakers.plain_english: If something goes seriously wrong (e.g. data loss or major service outage), the maximum amount of money you can recover from the Provider is limited to only 3 months of subscription fees.
deal_breakers.why_flagged:
1. Standard commercial software agreements provide a 12-month liability cap.
2. 3 months of fees provides almost no meaningful recovery for catastrophic operational harm.
3. Leaves Customer absorbing nearly all operational risk.
deal_breakers.suggested_negotiation: Customer proposes revising Section 9.2: Replace 'fees paid or payable... during the three months' with 'fees paid or payable... during the twelve (12) months preceding the event'.

clause_balance.provider_terms: Liability capped at 3 months of fees paid/payable.
clause_balance.customer_terms: Liability capped at 3 months of fees paid/payable (except payment obligations).
clause_balance.asymmetry_summary: Nominally mutual, but functionally protects the Provider as the service-delivering party while leaving customer recovery severely limited.

evidence.quote: each party’s aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed the fees paid or payable by Customer to Provider during the three months preceding the event giving rise to the claim.

watch_out.title: Retention of Backup Copies of Customer Data
watch_out.claim: Provider may retain backup copies of Customer Data for up to 180 days after deletion from production systems.
watch_out.plain_english: After you delete your data or end the contract, the Provider is legally permitted to keep backup copies of your sensitive company data in their systems for up to 180 days (6 months).
watch_out.why_flagged:
1. 180 days is an unusually long data retention window for deleted customer information.
2. Increases data exposure liability under modern privacy regulations (e.g. GDPR, DPDP).
3. Standard enterprise practice is 30 to 60 days maximum retention for disaster-recovery backups.
watch_out.suggested_negotiation: Customer proposes amending Section 4.4: Reduce the backup retention period from 'up to 180 days' to 'up to 30 days', followed by irreversible overwrite or destruction.

evidence.quote: Provider may retain backup copies of Customer Data for up to 180 days after deletion from production systems, provided such copies remain protected and are not restored except for disaster recovery purposes.

watch_out.title: Automatic Renewal and Non-Renewal Notice Period
watch_out.claim: The contract automatically renews unless either Party gives written notice of non-renewal at least 90 days before expiration.
watch_out.plain_english: The contract automatically renews for another full year unless you send an official written non-renewal notice at least 90 days before the contract expires.
watch_out.why_flagged:
1. Automatic 12-month lock-in without proactive reminder.
2. 90-day non-renewal window is easy to miss, locking the company into another year of fees.
watch_out.suggested_negotiation: Customer proposes reducing the non-renewal notice period from 90 days to 30 days, and adding an obligation for Provider to issue a reminder 60 days prior to renewal.

evidence.quote: Unless either Party gives written notice of non-renewal at least 90 days before expiration, the Agreement will automatically renew for successive 12-month periods.

watch_out.title: Customer's Security Audit Rights
watch_out.claim: Customer may audit Provider’s compliance with security obligations once per calendar year with 20 business days’ prior written notice, and Provider can provide third-party security reports to satisfy the audit request.
watch_out.plain_english: Customer may audit Provider’s compliance with security obligations once per calendar year with 20 business days’ prior written notice, and Provider can provide third-party security reports to satisfy the audit request.
watch_out.why_flagged: This matters because it defines the frequency and notice period for audits, as well as the option for the Provider to use third-party reports, which could impact the thoroughness of the audit process.
watch_out.suggested_negotiation: Consider specifying the criteria for what constitutes a 'reasonably sufficient' third-party report to ensure clarity on the adequacy of the audit process.

clause_balance.provider_terms: May substitute an independent report in lieu of granting direct audit access.
clause_balance.customer_terms: Restricted to once per calendar year upon 20 business days' advance notice.
clause_balance.asymmetry_summary: Customer's audit rights are tightly constrained in timing and can be satisfied with existing reports.

evidence.quote: Customer may, no more than once per calendar year and upon 20 business days’ prior written notice, audit Provider’s compliance with the security obligations in Section 4. Provider may satisfy the request by providing an independent third-party security report where reasonably sufficient to address the requested controls.

watch_out.title: Provider's Use of Customer's Name and Logo
watch_out.claim: The Provider can use the Customer's name and logo in presentations and marketing materials without prior consent.
watch_out.plain_english: The Provider can use your company's name and brand logo on their website and marketing materials without asking for your prior permission.
watch_out.why_flagged:
1. Unilateral publicity right without Customer marketing approval.
2. Risks brand association or disclosure of vendor relationship before launch.
watch_out.suggested_negotiation: Customer proposes amending Section 19: Add 'subject to Customer's prior written approval in each instance'.

evidence.quote: Provider may identify Customer by name and logo as a customer in Provider’s website, presentations, and marketing materials without obtaining additional approval from Customer.

protections.title: Provider's Responsibility for Subcontractors
protections.claim: Provider remains responsible for the acts and omissions of its subcontractors.
protections.plain_english: The Provider remains fully responsible for any mistakes, security breaches, or failures committed by its third-party subcontractors.
protections.why_flagged: This is a key protection: the vendor cannot evade liability by blaming an outsourced subprocessor.
protections.suggested_negotiation: Maintain this provision as drafted. It protects Customer interests.

evidence.quote: Provider remains responsible for the acts and omissions of its subcontractors to the same extent as if those acts or omissions were performed by Provider.

missing_clauses.title: Disaster Recovery SLA & RTO/RPO
missing_clauses.why_it_matters: The contract does not define explicit Recovery Time Objectives (RTO) or Recovery Point Objectives (RPO). If Provider suffers a catastrophic datacenter outage, there is no contractual commitment for when service or data will be restored.
missing_clauses.recommended_clause: Provider shall maintain a business continuity and disaster recovery plan with a Recovery Time Objective (RTO) of not more than 4 hours and a Recovery Point Objective (RPO) of not more than 1 hour.
missing_clauses.evidence_snippet: No disaster recovery SLA or RTO/RPO targets found.

missing_clauses.title: Maximum Security Incident Notification Window
missing_clauses.why_it_matters: Section 4.3 only requires notice 'without undue delay'. It lacks an explicit hour-based maximum window (e.g., within 24 to 72 hours). Without a strict timeframe, Customer may fail to meet mandatory regulatory reporting deadlines.
missing_clauses.recommended_clause: Provider shall notify Customer in writing without undue delay, and in any event within forty-eight (48) hours, after becoming aware of or confirming any Security Incident involving Customer Data.
missing_clauses.evidence_snippet: Section 4.3 specifies 'without undue delay', but omits an explicit hour-based SLA.

missing_clauses.title: Affirmative Data Deletion & Certification
missing_clauses.why_it_matters: The agreement permits Provider to retain backups for up to 180 days, but lacks an affirmative obligation for Provider to return all Customer Data upon expiration and certify permanent destruction in writing.
missing_clauses.recommended_clause: Within thirty (30) days of termination, Provider shall, at Customer's election, return or permanently and securely destroy all Customer Data, and deliver written certification of compliance signed by an officer of Provider.
missing_clauses.evidence_snippet: Permits 180-day backup retention, but lacks affirmative destruction certification.

missing_clauses.title: Advance Notice of New Subprocessors
missing_clauses.why_it_matters: Section 4.2 allows Provider to use subcontractors without prior notification or opportunity for Customer to object, which may violate Customer compliance standards or data residency policies.
missing_clauses.recommended_clause: Provider shall provide Customer with at least thirty (30) days' prior written notice before engaging any new subcontractor to process Customer Data, and Customer may object on reasonable security or compliance grounds.
missing_clauses.evidence_snippet: Section 4.2 permits subcontractors without advance notice or objection rights.

missing_clauses.title: Termination Right for Extended Force Majeure
missing_clauses.why_it_matters: Section 15 suspends liability during Force Majeure events, but gives Customer no right to terminate the contract if the outage or failure lasts for an extended period (e.g., longer than 30 consecutive days).
missing_clauses.recommended_clause: If a Force Majeure event prevents performance of the Services for more than thirty (30) consecutive days, Customer may terminate this Agreement immediately upon written notice without penalty.
missing_clauses.evidence_snippet: Section 15 suspends performance but provides no exit right for extended outages.

missing_clauses.title: Customer Convenience Termination Parity
missing_clauses.why_it_matters: Provider can terminate for convenience at any time upon 15 days' notice, but Customer is barred from terminating during the first 12 months and must provide 60 days' notice thereafter.
missing_clauses.recommended_clause: Either Party may terminate this Agreement for convenience at any time upon sixty (60) days' prior written notice.
missing_clauses.evidence_snippet: Section 10.4 locks Customer for 12 months with 60-day notice, while Section 10.3 allows Provider 15-day exit.

missing_clauses.title: Cyber Liability & E&O Insurance Commitments
missing_clauses.why_it_matters: The agreement contains no requirement for Provider to maintain Technology Errors & Omissions or Cyber Liability insurance to backstop its indemnification and security commitments.
missing_clauses.recommended_clause: Provider shall maintain commercial general liability insurance, technology errors & omissions, and cyber liability insurance with policy limits of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence during the Term.

risks.observation: Standard tier charges ₹12 per document overage, which is 140% higher than the Enterprise overage rate (₹5/doc). Unanticipated processing spikes could result in unpredictable monthly invoice surges.
risks.recommendation: Negotiate a monthly overage cap (e.g., maximum 20% over base fee) or an automatic tier bump mechanism when usage consistently exceeds included quota.

risks.risk_title: Absence of Price Protection / Cap on Renewal
risks.observation: The pricing table does not define annual fee adjustment limits (e.g. CPI or maximum 3-5% increase). Upon automatic renewal, Provider is not contractually restricted from raising monthly tier fees.
risks.recommendation: Insert a price escalation cap: 'Fees shall not increase by more than 3% annually upon renewal.'
